newsitem.title: UK: Nuclear fusion power coming next century.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear fusion power coming next century.

text.p: Nuclear fusion is a viable and clean energy source with a virtually limitless fuel supply but a commercial reactor to tame the power of the Hydrogen Bomb is still at least 30 years away, a senior official of Europe's fusion programme said.

"It's a long range option which contains the solution to all our energy problems," Alan Gibson, deputy director of the European Joint European Torus (JET) experimental project near Oxford told Reuters in an interview.
"We now have the fundamentals of a power source that we can control."
"I do see a day when fusion replaces oil and gas for electricity generation in the developed world... even if it will not replace oil for transportation fuels.
"The time scale could be, say, 30 to 50 years."

Starlight and sunlight are the product of fusion energy and the JET experimental programme has reproduced the process inside a doughnut-shaped device, reaching temperatures of 200 million degrees centigrade.

Since physical containers cannot hold the ionised plasma at such infernal temperatures, the JET device bottles it up in a doughnut or torus, the walls of which are made only of strong magnetic fields.
The fuel is deuterium, a heavy isotope of hydrogen widely found in water, and tritium, a still heavier form which is manufactured by the reactor itself. The by-product is helium, an inert gas.

Unlike nuclear fission -- which breaks apart heavy elements and is used in the A-Bomb and by present nuclear power plants -- the conditions needed for self-sustaining fusion are so delicate that any instability stops the reaction.
"With fusion, you blink and it goes out," Gibson said.
While the reactor itself becomes radioactive after prolonged use, it is short-lasting when compared to the radioactive products of nuclear fission.
The technical complexity of fusion means it will be costly when compared to fossil fuels today. But as moves to curb carbon emissions gather pace, it will become more attractive, Gibson said.
Initial achievements appear modest. One megawatt of thermal power was produced for two seconds in 1991, less than the energy input.
"We hope for 10 megawatts for three to five seconds," Gibson said. "We are gearing up now and it should happen this summer."
"Here at the level of JET we have about a fifth of the performance you need for the plasma to be self sustaining. You can't bridge this gap with JET - it is too small.
The similarly shaped Tokamak Fusion Test Reactor (TFTR) in California is another, less powerful, fusion device.
These, and other projects, are steps leading to construction of the first full-size experimental reactor - called ITER or International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor.
The development will be funded by the European Union, Russia, the United States and Japan and may be ready by 2008. A site has yet to be chosen and it is expected to cost some $6.6 billion to build.

ITER is expected to achieve "ignition" -- when the energy produced is enough to maintain the reaction -- and it may produce 1,500 megawatts of thermal power. It will also provide the technological springboard for the first demonstration commercial reactor, which could be ready as early as 2025.
"Probably the stage after ITER is when the question of cost will become all-important," Gibson said.
"To get from here to a system which could be at the heart of a power station we need a huge amount of technology and engineering development and advances in some areas of the physics."
"We now understand the problem of confinement pretty well but still when you go from the size of JET to the size of ITER the uncertainty in prediction of performance is a factor of two or three.
"Our experiments are like using a Wright Brothers aircraft to simulate a Jumbo Jet."
While the life of the programme has been extended until 1999, Gibson said JET could still operate in support of ITER after that.
JET has an annual budget of around $100 million and is the largest part of Europe's $500 million fusion research programme.

Japan adds another $390 million and the U.S. $370 million, according to 1995 figures published by the International Energy Agency (IEA.) Total world fusion research was around $1.1 billion in 1995, the IEA said.
"The JET programme runs at around half a percent of the total electricity generation cost in Europe," Gibson said. "This is a sustainable level for a long term project.

"Without doubt we can make fusion work. Whether or not we can make it work at a price that is economically competitive is a question still. If you take our most optimistic assumptions, it will be very reasonably priced.
"But if we continue to see environmental pressures acting against fossil fuels there may be pressure to speed up the fusion programme.
"Fusion can become available when society needs it."
